newsitem.title: UK: British woman loses bid for dead husband's sperm.
newsitem.headline: British woman loses bid for dead husband's sperm.

text.p: A young British widow lost her court battle on Thursday to have a baby through artificial insemination using her dead husband's sperm.

Diane Blood, 30, said she was "terribly upset" and would appeal the decision. "It just seems so terribly unnecessary, I can't understand why anyone would want to put me through it," she told a news conference.

"We planned a baby before he died. I just want that back. I don't see why my life as I planned it should have ended." In a case which sparked intense debate, Judge Stephen Brown, president of the court's family division, supported a refusal by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HEFA) to allow the insemination.
The regulatory body prevented Blood from using her husband's sperm because he had not given his written consent for its use before he died in March 1995 from bacterial meningitis.

Blood wept quietly in court as Brown announced the decision which prevents her from taking her husband's sperm -- being kept frozen in a British hospital -- to Belgium or the United States where doctors had already agreed to treat her.
"Mrs Blood has been advised by her lawyers she has very good grounds for appeal. We are hopeful the appeal will be decided early in the New Year," her solicitor Richard Stein said.
"This will allow Mrs. Blood to fulfill the wishes of her husband Stephen and their marriage vows without too much further delay."

Blood claimed she and her huband had been trying for a year to have a baby and that they had discussed the possibility of artificial insemination. The sperm was taken from him at her request while he was on a life-support system in a coma.
Brown said he had sympathy with Blood's predicament but was unable to overrule the HEFA's decision to refuse the procedure.
"The refusal to permit her so to do is for her in the nature of a double bereavement," he said.
"Nevertheless for the reasons of law that I have endeavoured to explain, I am unable to accede to this application."
The HEFA argued it was illegal under the 1990 Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act to allow the insemination procedure in Britain or abroad without her husband's written consent.
"Written consent was not available in this case, tragically, and we have always maintained that the law is quite clear in this regard," HEFA chairman Ruth Deech told reporters.
"We have every sympathy for Mrs. Blood but it was her husband's consent that was at issue and that was never given."
Blood said she was angry with the HEFA and the court for adhering so strictly to legislation that she believes is flawed.
"I think the law is crazy. They are putting a stop on something that is ultimately up to God," Blood said. "If I win my case it is still up to God whether I succeed medically."
Deech said it was up to parliament to decide whether or not new legislation was necessary. Deech, however, did not believe the law needed to be changed immediately:
"It is such a new law that I think it should be given a chance to be used and tested over a number of years."
Fertility experts reacted with dismay to today's ruling.
Dr Robert Forman, director of the London Gynaecology and Fertility Centre, said: "The judge has based his decision on the rules and compassion has gone out of the window."
